title: Paul Howard, Son of Three Stooges Legend Moe Howard, Dies at 91 – Hollywood Icon Remembered
body:
The entertainment world mourns the loss of Paul Howard, the 91‑year‑old son of legendary Three Stooges founder Moe Howard, who died peacefully in his New York City apartment on Tuesday. A lifelong steward of his father’s slap‑slap‑slap legacy, Paul spent decades nurturing the affection of Stooges fans, appearing at conventions, signing memorabilia and, most notably, serving as the narrator of the nine‑part documentary series “Hey Moe, Hey Dad!” that aired in 2015.

Born in 1933, Paul grew up in the shadow of one of America’s most iconic comedy trios. While his father’s on‑stage antics made household names of Larry, Curly, and Moe, the younger Howard learned early the importance of preserving that heritage. After Moe’s death in 1975, Paul assumed the unofficial role of family archivist, curating photographs, scripts, and personal anecdotes that would later become the backbone of the documentary series. The series, a collaboration between the Stooges’ estate and a boutique production house, combined rare archival footage with Paul’s warm, reflective commentary, offering both longtime aficionados and new audiences a behind‑the‑scenes look at the trio’s rise from vaudeville stages to silver‑screen legends.

Beyond the screen, Paul’s presence at fan conventions across the United States and abroad cemented his reputation as a bridge between the past and present. At events in Los Angeles, Chicago, and even Tokyo, he greeted admirers with the same geniality that characterized his father’s on‑stage persona. Attendees recall his willingness to share stories that had never been published, from Moe’s meticulous rehearsal routines to the troupe’s off‑camera camaraderie. “Meeting Paul felt like shaking hands with history,” said longtime Stooges collector Maria Alvarez, who met him at a 2018 convention in San Diego. “He didn’t just talk about the Stooges; he embodied the spirit of that era’s comedy.”

Industry observers note that Paul’s stewardship helped sustain the Three Stooges’ cultural relevance well into the digital age. The 2015 docuseries, which aired on a streaming platform, sparked a resurgence of interest that led to renewed merchandise lines, a limited‑edition vinyl release of the trio’s classic soundtracks, and a spike in streaming numbers for the Stooges’ original shorts. “His narration provided an authentic voice that resonated with both nostalgia‑driven fans and younger viewers discovering slapstick for the first time,” explained television historian Dr. Leonard Kim. “In an era where legacy acts often fade, Paul’s active participation kept the Stooges in the public conversation.”

Family members describe Paul as a modest, private individual who preferred the company of his grandchildren to the spotlight. He lived his later years on Manhattan’s Upper East Side, where he maintained a modest collection of memorabilia in a modest apartment that doubled as a mini‑museum. Despite his age, he continued to attend select conventions, often accompanied by his daughter, Susan Howard, who now oversees the family’s archival holdings. “Dad always said the best tribute to his work was simply to keep laughing,” Susan reflected. “He wanted the joy of the Stooges to live on, not just in museums, but in the everyday smiles of people.”

As the entertainment community reflects on Paul Howard’s passing, industry leaders anticipate a renewed effort to digitize and disseminate the Stooges’ extensive archives, a project Paul had championed in his final years. The family has announced plans to partner with a major streaming service to release a comprehensive, remastered collection of the trio’s short films, complete with previously unseen outtakes and commentary sourced from Paul’s personal notes. This initiative promises to introduce the timeless physical comedy of Moe, Larry, and Curly to a new generation, ensuring that the laughter that defined an era will continue to echo long after Paul Howard’s voice has been silenced.
